newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN OIL EXPLORATION SLOWLY GATHERS PACE.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN OIL EXPLORATION SLOWLY GATHERS PACE.

text.p: The exploration and development of South Africa's potential offshore oil and gas fields continues to slowly gather pace.

The country's first offshore oilfield is expected to start production by the end of April, while state-owned oil exploration company Soekor and Oklahoma-based Phillips International Exploration Inc are expected to finalise a prospecting lease for two large blocks within the next two months.
Soekor petroleum licensing unit manager Jack Holliday told Reuters that negotiations with Phillips for a prospecting lease for blocks 17 and 18 were now in their final stages.
This would give Phillips the right to actively explore for oil and gas in an area stretching from the Mozambican border to just south of Durban.
"The relevant documents will shortly be submitted to the Soekor board, the Mining Leases Board and the Minister of Minerals and Energy Affairs," he said.
"It is hoped that the contract will be signed during the next two months."
Soekor and Phillips signed a technical agreement in March last year granting the U.S. company the exclusive right to evaluate the oil and gas potential in the two blocks.
Asked about developments at the Oribi oilfield just off Mossel Bay, Soekor chief executive Joggie Heuser said that "considerable progress" had been made in preparing for production.
"All necessary sub-sea equipment has been installed and further preparatory operations are in progress, but we are experiencing some delays due to extreme weather conditions offshore," Heuser said.
"We are, however, still planning for first oil production at the end of April."
Energy Africa , which has a 20 percent stake in the oilfield, recently said it expected production to start in May, mainly because of the rough weather conditions.
An oil rig, the Orca, was refurbished at Simon's Town harbour and towed up the coast and is now at the well site.
Oribi, which is about 140 km south-west of Mossel Bay, is expected to initially produce 20,000 barrels of oil a day, with this amount tapering off over three to six years.
It will form the nucleus for the subsequent development of several other nearby oil discoveries, which would extend production life by a further six years.
Soekor plans to pump the oil into a one million barrel shuttle tanker for shipment to one of South Africa's three coastal refineries in Cape Town or Durban.
